prompt: Why must UIKit/AppKit views only be mutated from the main thread?
choices: UIView and CALayer mutations are batched into an implicit transaction committed by the main run loop before each display refresh; concurrent mutation corrupts that pending transaction
Swift's automatic reference counting is not thread-safe for any object
UIKit holds a single global lock on the entire view hierarchy that would cause contention if used from multiple threads
Apple disabled multithreaded UI updates to simplify debugging in Xcode

prompt: In the React Native old-bridge deadlock described in this module, what is the exact lock-ordering pattern that causes the hang?
choices: The JS thread leaks memory until the app is killed by the OS for excessive memory use
The main thread blocks synchronously waiting on the JS thread, while the JS thread simultaneously blocks synchronously waiting on the main thread (an AB-BA deadlock)
The Shadow thread computes an infinite Yoga layout loop that never resolves
The JS thread crashes with a stack overflow from recursive bridge calls

prompt: A Flutter MethodChannel handler blocks Android's main Looper for 8 seconds doing synchronous file I/O. What user-visible failure results, and why does iOS have no exact equivalent?
choices: An ANR dialog, because Android's system server (a separate process) can paint a wait/kill dialog over the frozen app; iOS runs one process per app with no such external surface, so it silently kills the app via the watchdog instead
A kernel panic, because Android treats UI thread blocks as fatal system errors
Nothing happens on Android either, since Looper-based threading tolerates indefinite blocking by design
The app automatically restarts on both platforms with no dialog shown

prompt: Since Android 10's Scoped Storage, why can't a cross-platform file-picker plugin return a plain filesystem path on Android the way it can on iOS?
choices: Android deprecated the File class entirely in favor of a string-based API
Scoped Storage routes access to other apps' files through content:// URIs resolved via ContentResolver, which may have no backing path on disk at all, unlike iOS's container-relative file:// paths
Android file paths are always encrypted and cannot be represented as strings
iOS also stopped returning real paths at the same time, making this no longer a real divergence

prompt: What OS-level mechanism do iOS App Extensions within the same app use to share data without inter-process IPC, and what is Android's structurally closest equivalent?
choices: iOS uses an App Group's shared container directory; Android's closest equivalent is a ContentProvider exposed over Binder IPC between components
Both platforms use the exact same shared-memory API, since both are POSIX-based
iOS uses XPC exclusively for this; Android has no comparable mechanism at all
iOS apps share data via public cloud sync only; there is no local mechanism

prompt: Why does iOS require schemes to be pre-declared in LSApplicationQueriesSchemes before calling canOpenURL:, while Android's queryIntentActivities() allows open-ended discovery of installed apps?
choices: iOS treats enumerating installed apps as a sensitive, fingerprinting-adjacent capability and restricts it to an explicit allowlist; Android's Binder-mediated Intent system treats declared capabilities as open, queryable by design
Android's PackageManager API is simply older and was never updated for privacy
LSApplicationQueriesSchemes is an App Store review formality with no runtime enforcement
Both platforms behave identically at runtime; the difference is purely in compile-time tooling

prompt: A shared Rust core (built with uniffi-rs) calls a callback trait implemented in Swift and Kotlin to notify the UI of a state change. Why must both the Swift and Kotlin binding code hop onto their respective main thread/Looper before updating a view, even though the Rust core itself has no concept of 'main thread'?
choices: UniFFI automatically performs the hop inside the generated Rust code, so this is unnecessary in practice
The Rust core runs the callback on whatever thread triggered it, and the OS-level main-thread-only UI rule still applies regardless of what layer initiated the call
Rust callbacks are always already running on the main thread by construction
This hop is only needed on Android; iOS callbacks are thread-safe for UIKit by default

prompt: Why can't a cross-platform framework offer one unified 'share this file with another app' API that behaves identically on iOS and Android under the hood?
choices: Because the underlying OS sandbox primitives genuinely differ in kind, not just in syntax: Android's Binder/Intent/ContentProvider system allows open declared-capability discovery and content-URI-based access grants, while iOS mediates everything through pre-declared schemes, extensions, and security-scoped URLs
Because Dart and JavaScript cannot call native file APIs at all, only Kotlin and Swift can
Because sharing files is disabled by default on both platforms for security reasons
Because this is purely a historical limitation that modern framework versions have already fully resolved with one shared implementation
